To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the maximum transpiration rate of sympatric species of oaks is co-ordinated with soil moisture availability through changes in allometry; and (ii) the vulnerability of oaks to freeze-induced cavitation varies among species and evolutionary lineages.
the allometry of hydraulic traits is an important mechanism that allows co-ordination of water transport capacity with the soil water regime.
the hydraulic properties of oaks in northern central Florida are strongly influenced by habitat and phylogenetic history.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of habitat and evolutionary lineage on the hydraulic properties of oaks.
the effects of habitat and evolutionary history on the hydraulic properties of sympatric species.
the co-ordination of water transport capacity in oaks with soil water availability and with the evolution of freezing tolerance in oaks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the hydraulic architecture of sympatric oaks in northern central Florida is strongly influenced by habitat, leaf habit, phylogenetic lineage, and the interaction of these factors.
the hydraulic properties and freeze‐thaw induced embolism of oaks are strongly influenced by the species’ leaf habit, habitat and evolutionary lineage.

evergreen species, on average and in general, had greater maximum transpiration, lower vulnerability to freezing, greater K _{L}, greater maximum hydraulic conductivity, greater specific conductivity, and lower Huber values than deciduous species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the differences in freezing‐induced embolism among species were largely explained by differences in allometry (leaf area per shoot, Huber values) and vessel diameter, whereas the differences in hydraulic conductance among species were explained by differences in leaf area per shoot.
the evergreen oaks of the southeastern United States have evolved a combination of traits that allow them to maintain higher K L and lower vulnerability to freezing than deciduous oaks.
species with higher maximum K L and lower Huber values are better able to maintain high leaf water potentials in the face of drought, and are therefore better adapted to dry habitats.

species with different leaf habits can have similar water transport properties and vulnerability to freezing if the two species occur in different habitats and/or belong to different evolutionary lineages.
